title: Boss: on call
summary: Three production incidents on a real Docker Engine: a slow starter marked unhealthy, a morning-after deploy, and memory pressure.

steps.title: The pager goes off
body: Production incidents start as a symptom on a dashboard or a page from on-call. Each one below opens its own machine
with a **real Docker Engine** and the incident already happening. Your tools: `docker ps -a`, `docker logs`,
`docker inspect -f`, `docker stats --no-stream`, `docker update`, and running containers again with the right flags.

steps.title: Incident 1: "search is unhealthy, but it works"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. The container `search` is marked `(unhealthy)`, yet
`docker exec search wget -qO- http://localhost:9200/health` answers `ok` now. On the cluster this would mean an
Find out why (its log and its health history tell the story), then replace `search` (same name, same image, same
probe command, interval, timeout and retries) with one that becomes **healthy** on its own and stays healthy.

checks.name: search is healthy
checks.fail: `search` is not healthy. While it builds its index the probe fails: give the healthcheck a start period.

checks.name: the probe is unchanged
checks.fail: Keep the probe command, the 1 s interval and the 3 retries: only the start period is missing.

checks.name: its start period covers the 8-second warm-up
checks.cmd: docker inspect search | jq -r '.[0].Config.Healthcheck.StartPeriod // 0 | if . >= 8000000000 then "ok" else "start period: \(. / 1e9) s" end'
checks.fail: The start period should cover the 8-second index build: `--health-start-period 15s`.

hints: `docker logs search` says how long it takes to start; `docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health}}' search | jq` shows the failed probes.
With a 1 s interval and 3 retries it is declared unhealthy after about 3 seconds, long before the index is ready.
`docker rm -f search`, then the same `docker run` with `--health-start-period 15s` added (see `docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Healthcheck}}' search` for the rest).
solution: docker run -d --name search --health-cmd 'wget -qO- http://localhost:9200/health || exit 1' --health-interval 1s --health-timeout 1s --health-retries 3 --health-start-period 15s shop/search:3.1
steps.explain: Once a container is marked unhealthy, nothing in Docker marks it healthy again until a probe passes, and orchestrators act on that status by restarting it, which with a slow starter becomes a restart loop that never finishes starting. The start period is the grace period for warm-up: failures in it do not count, and the first success ends it. Kubernetes splits the same idea out as a `startupProbe`.

steps.title: Incident 2: "the morning after the deploy"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. After last night's deploy only `web` is still up; `thumbnails`, `mailer`
and `status` are down. Each one has a different cause. Find each cause and run each container again (same name,
same image) so that all four **stay up**:
- `thumbnails` (`shop/thumbnails:1.0`) needs about 24 MB of working memory;
- `mailer` should run its image's **own** default command;

checks.name: all four are running
checks.cmd: for c in web thumbnails mailer status; do docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} {{.State.Running}}' $c; done

checks.name: thumbnails got enough memory and is ready
checks.cmd: docker logs thumbnails 2>&1 | tail -n 1; docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' thumbnails
checks.fail: `thumbnails` should log `ready` without being OOM-killed: give it a higher limit (64 MB, say).

checks.name: mailer runs the image's own command
checks.cmd: docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Cmd}} {{.State.Running}}' mailer && docker logs mailer | tail -n 1
checks.fail: `mailer` does not run `mail-relay`, its image's default command (`docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Cmd}}' shop/mailer:1.0`).

checks.name: status keeps httpd in the foreground
checks.cmd: docker exec status ps -o args | grep '[h]ttpd'

hints: `docker ps -a` and `docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' NAME` sort the three: memory, a missing command, a process that ended.
Run arguments after the image replace its CMD: leave them out to get the default back.

`docker run -d --name thumbnails --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m shop/thumbnails:1.0`, plain `docker run -d --name mailer shop/mailer:1.0`, and `docker run -d --name status busybox:1.37 httpd -f -p 80`.
solution: docker inspect -f '{{.Name}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}' thumbnails mailer status
steps.explain: Three exits, three meanings: 137 with `OOMKilled` (the limit is too small for the working set), 127 (an overridden command that does not exist in this image), and 0 (a server that put itself in the background). Note that every fix meant **recreating** the container: a container's command and most of its flags are fixed when it is created, which is why teams keep them in a compose file or a script instead of in someone's shell history.

steps.title: Incident 3: "memory alerts are firing"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal with four services, each with a memory limit. Monitoring says some of them
1. Write into `~/answers/pressure.txt` the names (one per line) of the containers using **70% or more** of their
2. Give the **worst** one room without restarting it: raise its limit to **128 MB** (no extra swap).

checks.name: pressure.txt lists the containers at 70% or more
checks.cmd: diff <(docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}} {{.MemPerc}}' | tr -d '%' | awk '$2 >= 70 || ($1 == "worker") {print $1}' | sort) <(sed '/^$/d' ~/answers/pressure.txt | sort -u)
checks.fail: Not the right list. `docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}} {{.MemUsage}} {{.MemPerc}}'` shows usage against each limit.

checks.name: worker's limit is 128 MB, no extra swap
checks.fail: `worker` (the worst) should now have a 128 MB limit with `--memory-swap` equal, still running, never restarted. `docker update`.

checks.name: the others keep their limits
checks.fail: Only the worst container should change.

hints: `docker stats --no-stream` shows `MEM USAGE / LIMIT` and `MEM %` for every container.
`--format '{{.Name}} {{.MemPerc}}'` gives one easy line each; compare with 70.
steps.explain: `docker stats` reads the same cgroup counters the kernel's OOM killer uses, so "90% of the limit" is a real warning: the next spike gets the container killed with 137. `docker update` buys time without a restart; the lasting fix is the right limit in the compose file (or finding the leak). Note that memory written to tmpfs (`/dev/shm` here) counts against the limit too, a classic surprise.
